title: CONGENITAL MYOPATHY 10B, MILD VARIANT
alt_titles: MYOPATHY, AREFLEXIA, RESPIRATORY DISTRESS, AND DYSPHAGIA, EARLY-ONSET, MILD VARIANT

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that the mild variant of congenital myopathy-10B (CMYO10B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene on chromosome 5.

checks.claim: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10B (CMYO10B) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Early-onset myopathy, areflexia, respiratory distress, and dysphagia (EMARDD) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEGF10 gene (OMIM #614399). Phenotypic spectrum of EMARDD is variable, ranging from severe infantile forms
checks.explanation: The paper places the mild variant within the MEGF10 spectrum and says milder patients carry homozygous or compound heterozygous missense variants.

checks.claim: The MEGF10 gene is located on chromosome 5.
checks.evidence_quote: MEGF10 lies within a linkage peak on chromosome 5 that reached the maximum possible LOD score of 1.329.
checks.explanation: The paper places MEGF10 on chromosome 5.

paragraphs.text: The mild variant of congenital myopathy-10B (CMYO10B) is a muscle disorder that is milder than the classic early-onset form. Features include axial and proximal muscle weakness, joint contractures, scoliosis, and respiratory insufficiency that begins in childhood or later. Muscle biopsy may show minicores along with dystrophic or myofibrillar changes (Boyden et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2018; Croci et al., 2022).

checks.evidence_quote: The phenotypes described therein are generally similar to those of families 1030 and 105, but are more severe.
checks.explanation: The paper says the previously reported null-mutation families were more severe than its own patients.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) reported a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family of mixed European ancestry (family 1030) in which 3 of 4 sibs had an unclassified myopathy. Weakness began by 12 months of age, first in the neck. It was mainly axial and proximal, included facial weakness, and stabilized in adolescence. Neck contractures appeared in infancy, and contractures of the elbows, knees, and heel cords developed by adulthood. Serum CK measured before age 10 years was mildly elevated. All 3 patients had childhood-onset scoliosis treated with spinal fusion. Beginning at age 10 to 11 years, all developed respiratory problems treated with nighttime bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation. One patient was born with cleft palate, a second had a midline ridge on her palate, and all 3 had hypernasal speech. Muscle biopsies showed dystrophic features, including fatty replacement, increased perimysial and endomysial connective tissue, and isolated regenerating fibers. They also showed moth-eaten fibers and minicores, a slight type I fiber predominance, and marked variation in fiber size.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) also reported a Caucasian female of distant Portuguese ancestry (subject 105-1) who had been diagnosed with multiminicore disease. At several weeks of age she presented with hypotonia, a weak neck, and a floppy head. She also had a markedly high-arched palate, failure to thrive due to poor feeding, blue-tinged sclerae, and hyperflexible joints. As a child she had frequent acute pulmonary infections but no chronic breathing problems. At age 10 years her serum CK was 302 U/L and she had mild scoliosis, which progressed to 20 degrees by age 12 years. Muscle biopsy showed fiber size variation, internalized nuclei, and slightly increased endomysial connective tissue. Electron microscopy confirmed minicores.

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) reported a 22-year-old Italian man born to consanguineous parents at 33 weeks' gestation. He had weak suction, and elbow contractures and scoliosis were present from the first months of life. Motor development was not delayed. He developed slowly progressive muscle weakness with impaired walking, rhinolalia, and dysphagia. Respiratory involvement required nocturnal noninvasive ventilation from age 16 years, and from age 17 years he had recurrent pulmonary infections due to aspiration. On examination he had axial hypotonia, generalized muscle hypotrophy and weakness, cleft palate, global areflexia, contractures of the elbows and ankles, hyperlordosis, and an equinovarus foot stance. Serum CK was normal. A first muscle biopsy at age 5 years showed nonspecific changes: fiber size variation, internal nuclei, and fibrosis. A later biopsy showed whorled fibers, cytoplasmic inclusions, and minicores.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) performed whole-genome sequencing in an affected member of family 1030, filtered by linkage data. In the 3 affected sibs they identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the MEGF10 gene: C326R and C774R. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the mutations were in trans and segregated with the disorder in all 6 family members. Both mutations were absent from dbSNP, 1000 Genomes Project, and NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project data, and from more than 645 genotyped controls. Each substitution affected a cysteine of an atypical EGF-like domain that is conserved in 43 species. Boyden et al. (2012) then screened the MEGF10 open reading frame in 190 additional patients with unexplained myopathies. Subject 105-1 carried a heterozygous c.211C-T mutation predicting an arg71-to-trp (R71W) substitution in the emilin domain, inherited from an unaffected parent. No second mutation was found, including in RT-PCR products from muscle RNA. Boyden et al. (2012) suggested that this patient may carry a second MEGF10 mutation they were unable to detect.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) noted that the C774R mutation found in their family 1030 had also been reported, in compound heterozygosity with a frameshift mutation, in a family with a more severe phenotype. They proposed that the milder disease in their patients was consistent with residual MEGF10 function from missense mutations, compared with total loss of MEGF10 expression in families with null mutations. They also noted that minicores were prominent in their patients but had not been reported in patients with null mutations.

checks.claim: Boyden et al. (2012) noted that the MEGF10 C774R mutation found in family 1030 had also been reported, in compound heterozygosity with a frameshift mutation, in a family with a more severe phenotype.
checks.evidence_quote: One reported family was compound heterozygous for the c.2320T > C (p.C774R) missense mutation we identified in family 1030 and a frameshift mutation. The phenotypes described therein are generally similar to those of families 1030 and 105, but are more severe.

checks.claim: Boyden et al. (2012) proposed that the milder disease in family 1030 was consistent with residual MEGF10 function from missense mutations, compared with total loss of MEGF10 expression in families with null mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: This difference is consistent with the total loss of detectable MEGF10 expression observed in the reported families, compared to the expected misfolding of MEGF10 protein due to disruption of disulfide bonds in family 1030. Accordingly, affected members of family 1030 may retain a small amount of residual MEGF10 function

checks.claim: Boyden et al. (2012) noted that minicores were prominent in their patients but had not been reported in patients with MEGF10 null mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: minicores were not noted in the biopsies from the reported families with null mutations but were a prominent feature in our patients with missense mutations.

paragraphs.text: Takayama et al. (2016) found a homozygous frameshift mutation in a Japanese patient with the severe EMARDD phenotype. A second Japanese patient with the milder phenotype carried a splice site mutation and a cysteine missense mutation. The authors concluded that these cases indicated a genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.

checks.claim: Takayama et al. (2016) found a homozygous MEGF10 frameshift mutation in a Japanese patient with the severe EMARDD phenotype.
checks.evidence_quote: one with EMARDD phenotype who had a novel homozygous frameshift mutation, c.131_132del
checks.explanation: A homozygous frameshift mutation was found in the patient with the EMARDD phenotype. The abstract contrasts EMARDD with the milder phenotype, which fits the draft's word 'severe'.

checks.claim: A second Japanese patient with the milder phenotype reported by Takayama et al. (2016) carried a MEGF10 splice site mutation and a cysteine missense mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: the other with the milder phenotype who harbored a compound heterozygous mutation, c.2981-2A > G, and a novel missense mutation, p.Cys810Tyr
checks.explanation: The second patient had the splice-site variant plus a missense change at a cysteine (Cys810Tyr).

checks.claim: Takayama et al. (2016) concluded that their cases indicated a genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: This is the first report on East Asian patients with MEGF10 myopathy showing two phenotypes, indicating the genotype-phenotype correlation in MEGF10 myopathy.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this conclusion directly.

paragraphs.text: Harris et al. (2018) reviewed 20 reported patients with MEGF10 mutations and confirmed a genotype-phenotype correlation. In patients with at least 1 null mutation, respiratory dysfunction began in the first year of life. In patients with 2 missense mutations, it began at 10 years of age or much later.

checks.claim: Harris et al. (2018) reviewed 20 reported patients with MEGF10 mutations and confirmed a genotype-phenotype correlation.
checks.evidence_quote: We performed a detailed review of all reported MEGF10 cases (n = 20), and confirmed the presence of a genotype-phenotype correlation

checks.claim: In patients with at least 1 MEGF10 null mutation, respiratory dysfunction began in the first year of life.
checks.evidence_quote: with ≥1 null mutation onset of respiratory dysfunction occurs in the first year of life

checks.claim: In patients with 2 MEGF10 missense mutations, respiratory dysfunction began at 10 years of age or much later.
checks.evidence_quote: whereas with 2 missense mutations, respiratory dysfunction occurs at 10 years old or much later

paragraphs.text: Croci et al. (2022) observed that their patient had a homozygous missense mutation but early-onset, progressive disease. Minicores appeared only on a later biopsy. The authors proposed that the minicores that mark the late-onset group may result from long-standing myofibrillar pathology that begins in infancy, and they suggested a phenotypic continuum rather than a dichotomy between the severe and mild forms.

checks.claim: Croci et al. (2022) observed that their patient had a homozygous MEGF10 missense mutation but early-onset, progressive disease.
checks.evidence_quote: Although our patient carried a missense variant, he displayed an early-onset myopathy with progressive course.

checks.claim: In the patient reported by Croci et al. (2022), minicores appeared only on a later muscle biopsy.
checks.evidence_quote: The first muscle biopsy performed at age 5 years revealed unspecific muscle damage, whereas the second biopsy performed one year later showed more definite and significant alterations, suggestive of a myofibrillar myopathy with presence of core like areas
checks.explanation: The first biopsy was nonspecific and the later biopsy showed minicores.

checks.claim: Croci et al. (2022) proposed that the minicores that mark the late-onset MEGF10 myopathy group may result from long-standing myofibrillar pathology that begins in infancy.
checks.evidence_quote: we propose that minicores that mark the late onset group, can actually be a consequence of a longstanding myofibrillar pathological processes starting in infancy.

checks.claim: Croci et al. (2022) suggested a phenotypic continuum rather than a dichotomy between the severe and mild forms of MEGF10 myopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: our report proposes a continuum in the phenotypes associated with MEGF10 variants, which include a clinical and histopathological progression of the disease and represent a novelty from the dichotomy between the early onset classic severe EMARDD and mvEMARDD.

paragraphs.text: Boyden et al. (2012) knocked down megf10 in zebrafish with 4 different splice-blocking morpholinos. The morphants had unhatched eggs, curled or bent tails, impaired swimming, and reduced motility in response to touch. They also showed decreased birefringence, disrupted somite boundaries, gaps between myofibers, and myofibrillar disorganization on electron microscopy, consistent with a myopathic process.

checks.claim: megf10 zebrafish morphants had unhatched eggs.
checks.evidence_quote: knockdown of megf10 in zebrafish by four different morpholinos resulted in abnormal phenotypes including unhatched eggs, curved tails, impaired motility, and disorganized muscle tissue

checks.claim: The findings in megf10 zebrafish morphants were consistent with a myopathic process.

paragraphs.text: In 3 sibs from a nonconsanguineous Caucasian family with a congenital myopathy with minicores (CMYO10B), Boyden et al. (2012) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the MEGF10 gene. One allele was a c.976T-C transition in exon 10, resulting in a cys326-to-arg (C326R) substitution in EGF-like domain 6. The other was C774R. The mutations were found by whole-genome sequencing, confirmed in trans by Sanger sequencing, and segregated with the disorder. C326R was absent from 715 controls and public databases. The affected cysteine is conserved in 43 species and was predicted to form a disulfide bond.

checks.evidence_quote: the heterozygous missense mutations c.976T > C (p.C326R) and c.2320T > C (p.C774R) in MEGF10, the sole remaining candidate, were confirmed by Sanger sequencing to be in trans in affected subjects
checks.explanation: Supported; elsewhere the family is described as non-consanguineous Caucasian with 3 affected sibs and a myopathy with minicores.

checks.evidence_quote: Affected subjects were compound heterozygous for missense mutations c.976T > C (p.C326R) and c.2320T > C (p.C774R).

The mutation was in compound heterozygosity with C326R. It was absent from 645 controls and public databases, and the affected cysteine is conserved in 43 species. Boyden et al. (2012) noted that the same mutation had been reported in compound heterozygosity with a frameshift mutation in a family with a more severe phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In a 22-year-old Italian man with a progressive form of mild variant EMARDD (CMYO10B), born to consanguineous parents, Croci et al. The mutation was found by exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and both parents were heterozygous.
